relationship: Hezekiah son of Ahaz receives his own accession heading
rationale: The earlier Ahaz closure names Hezekiah his son succeeding him; the new heading again identifies Hezekiah son of Ahaz over Judah. The third-Hoshea-year synchronism remains the heading’s own additional statement.

relationship: Hezekiah’s accession age and Jerusalem reign agree in the two notices
rationale: Both give Hezekiah twenty-five at accession and twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. Abou daughter of Zechariah and Abba daughter of Zacharias remain their respective maternal forms without a newly certified name equation.

relationship: Hezekiah’s right-conduct assessment expressly invokes David
rationale: Both assess Hezekiah as doing right before the Lord according to everything David his father did. This particular shared royal model does not independently certify every action in either reign narrative.

relationship: Manasseh’s later rebuilding explicitly reverses Hezekiah’s high-place removal
rationale: Hezekiah removes high places and destroys groves; the later Manasseh notice expressly says he rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah pulled down. The later Baal and heavenly-host clauses do not become additions to Hezekiah’s stated actions.

relationship: Moses’s bronze serpent is named in its making and later destruction
rationale: Kings explicitly calls the destroyed bronze serpent the one Moses made and reports later incense to it. Numbers narrates Moses making a bronze serpent for the stated looking-and-living provision; it does not narrate the later incense or Hezekiah’s destruction.

relationship: Hezekiah’s hope and wholehearted service receive distinct positive summaries
rationale: Kings says Hezekiah hoped in the Lord and gives its unparalleled-kings assessment; Chronicles says he sought his God with his whole soul in the stated house, law and ordinance work. The related devotion summaries retain their different scopes and comparative wording.

relationship: Clinging to the Lord follows the explicit cleave-to-Him command
rationale: Kings describes Hezekiah clinging to the Lord and keeping the commands given Moses; Deuteronomy commands fearing, serving and cleaving to the Lord. The shared allegiance action is compared without claiming the king’s notice quotes every command in that target.

relationship: Same-chapter The break with Assyria is later invoked in the envoy’s challenge
rationale: The narrator reports Hezekiah breaking with Assyria and not serving its king; the envoy later asks on whom he trusts that he has broken with him. The narrator’s Lord-with-him assessment remains distinct from the envoy’s accusatory question.

relationship: Foreigners attacking Judah precede Hezekiah’s campaign against foreigners
rationale: Kings reports Hezekiah striking the foreigners to Gaza and its boundary; Chronicles earlier describes foreigners capturing and settling Judah’s cities. The reversal in military direction is compared without equating every listed city with Gaza or independently reconstructing a single campaign.

relationship: The Samaria siege is repeated with named king and additional synchronisms
rationale: Both accounts place the Assyrian advance and siege of Samaria in Hoshea’s story; the earlier text names Salamanasar and gives the three-year siege. Salamanassar and the added Hezekiah-Hoshea year synchronisms remain the later notice’s supplied wording.

relationship: Samaria’s capture is expressly located in Hoshea’s ninth year
rationale: Both place Samaria’s capture in Hoshea’s ninth year. The later notice also gives Hezekiah’s sixth year and the end-of-three-years wording, without a new calculation that replaces either actual chronological statement.

relationship: Samaria’s deportation and named destinations are recalled
rationale: Both deport the captured Samaria population to the Assyrians and name Alae, Abor, Gozan and Ore of the Medes. The later Abor-river and earlier rivers wording remain distinct instead of a newly harmonized geographical list.

relationship: The deportation explanations name covenant disobedience and forbidden service
rationale: Kings explains the fall by not listening to the Lord or doing Moses’s commands; the earlier explanation specifies sin, other gods and service forbidden by the Lord. These are particular explanations of the same fall, without supplying an unreported exhaustive list of transgressions.

relationship: Sennacherib’s fortified-city campaign shares the fourteenth-year setting
rationale: Both date Sennacherib’s capture of the fortified cities to Hezekiah’s fourteenth year. Judah and Judea remain the supplied territorial wording, and neither notice is expanded into a reconstructed campaign calendar.

relationship: Same-chapter The imposed silver-and-gold demand is followed by the reported transfer
rationale: Hezekiah offers to bear the Assyrian king’s demand, which is stated as three hundred silver talents and thirty gold talents; the following units describe silver and gilded structural material given. Those transfer notices do not independently recount the exact demanded weights as paid amounts.

relationship: Same-chapter The house and treasury silver follows the stated Assyrian imposition
rationale: Hezekiah gives the silver found in the Lord’s and king’s houses after the Assyrian king imposes silver and gold. The source names the actual silver supply, while the target preserves the demanded figures rather than a new audited payment total.

relationship: Same-chapter Gilded doors and supports are given after the gold demand
rationale: Hezekiah cuts apart the gilded sanctuary doors and fixed supports and gives them to Assyria’s king; the earlier imposition included thirty talents of gold. The specific material action is linked to that demand without measuring the recovered gold or inventing an assay.

relationship: The Lachish-to-Jerusalem envoy stands at the upper-pool aqueduct
rationale: Both describe a large force sent from Lachish or Lachis to Hezekiah at Jerusalem and the upper-pool aqueduct by the fuller’s field. Kings additionally names Tharthan and Raphis alongside Rhapsakes; Isaiah’s Rapsakes wording is not expanded to repeat those names.

relationship: The steward, scribe and recorder form the corresponding receiving delegation
rationale: Both name Eliakim son of Chelkias the steward, Somnas the scribe and the son of Asaph as recorder. Joash and Joach remain the respective forms, and Kings’s preceding call to Hezekiah is not added to Isaiah’s shorter meeting notice.

relationship: The Assyrian great-king speech opens by questioning Hezekiah’s trust
rationale: Rhapsakes or Rapsakes directs the delegation to tell Hezekiah the great Assyrian king’s question about trust. The matching named speech framework does not make the king’s challenge the narrator’s own verdict on Hezekiah.

relationship: Counsel, words of lips and the trust challenge recur with different syntax
rationale: Both speeches connect counsel or lip-words with war and ask whom Hezekiah trusts in his resistance. Kings’s quoted counsel-and-strength wording and broken-with-me clause remain distinct from Isaiah’s battle-line question and disobey-me wording.

relationship: Egypt is compared with a broken reed staff that enters the supporting hand
rationale: Both speeches call Egypt a broken reed staff and connect leaning upon it with injury to the hand, then name Pharaoh and those trusting him. Kings’s additional piercing wording remains its own clause rather than a new physical experiment.

relationship: The Assyrian accusation invokes Hezekiah’s removed altars and single altar
rationale: Both Assyrian speeches appeal to Hezekiah removing high places or altars and directing worship before one altar. Chronicles adds burning incense there; the accusation remains hostile speech and does not establish that the Lord condemned Hezekiah’s reform.

relationship: The two-thousand-horse offer is conditional on providing riders
rationale: Both speeches offer two thousand horses if Hezekiah’s side can provide riders. The matching count and condition are retained as the envoy’s challenge, without inventing an accepted transfer or a verified rider total.

relationship: The district-governor challenge accompanies reliance on Egypt’s mounted force
rationale: Both ask how Hezekiah could face a district governor and refer to trust in Egypt for mounted military help. Kings’s least-servant and chariot clauses and Isaiah’s servants wording are retained in their actual different forms.

relationship: The envoy asks whether the Assyrian advance was without the Lord
rationale: Both speeches ask whether they came against the country without the Lord. Kings additionally quotes an asserted Lord-command to destroy the land; that assertion remains the envoy’s claim and is not inserted into Isaiah’s shorter rhetorical question.

relationship: The delegation requests Syrian rather than Judean within the wall audience’s hearing
rationale: Both have the named officials ask for Syrian, which they understand, and object to Judean being heard by the people on the wall. The language labels and the audience are preserved without substituting modern language names.

relationship: The envoy explicitly includes the wall audience in his dung-and-urine threat
rationale: Both speeches challenge whether the message is only for the rulers and include those sitting on the wall who would eat dung and drink urine together with them. The threatened condition is not converted into a separately narrated event already occurring.

relationship: The envoy loudly addresses the audience in Judean with the great king’s words
rationale: Both have Rhapsakes or Rapsakes stand and call loudly in Judean to hear the great Assyrian king’s words. The deliberate public address corresponds without an invented response by the people.

relationship: The king’s warning denies Hezekiah’s capacity to rescue
rationale: Both speeches warn against Hezekiah’s words and deny rescue through them or him. Kings’s lift-you-up and from-my-hand wording remains distinct from Isaiah’s deceive-you wording; neither is adopted as an independent narrator’s conclusion.

relationship: The anti-confidence warning quotes a Lord-rescue and city-deliverance promise
rationale: Both Assyrian speeches tell the audience not to accept Hezekiah’s assurance that God will rescue and the city will not enter the Assyrian king’s hand. The quoted assurance and the speaker opposing it remain distinguishable.

relationship: The invitation to come out offers vine, fig tree and cistern provision
rationale: Both speeches tell the people not to listen to Hezekiah and invite them out with vine, fig-tree and cistern provisions. Make a blessing and if you wish to be blessed remain different invitations, and Kings’s drinking-from-vine wording is not silently changed to Isaiah’s eating.

relationship: The proposed transfer to a similar land accompanies rejection of promised rescue
rationale: Both speeches promise removal to a similar land of grain, wine, bread and vineyards and reject Hezekiah’s rescue assurance. Kings additionally names oil-bearing olives, honey and live-not-die wording; those promises remain the envoy’s speech rather than an accomplished resettlement.

relationship: The nations’ gods are challenged over rescue from Assyria
rationale: Both speeches ask whether each nation’s god rescued its country from the Assyrian king. The repeated argument remains the hostile king’s challenge, without an independent finding that the Lord is one of those defeated gods.

relationship: Named-city gods and Samaria appear in the repeated rescue challenge
rationale: Both speeches name Aimath and the Arphad or Arphath setting, another supplied city form, and Samaria in the rescue challenge. Seppharouain and Seppharim’s city remain distinct forms without certifying every geographical equation.

relationship: The final challenge explicitly turns from other lands to Jerusalem
rationale: Both speeches conclude by asking which gods rescued their lands so that God should rescue Jerusalem. The parallel argument is preserved as the envoy’s inference rather than a statement that Jerusalem was captured.

relationship: The audience’s silence expressly follows the king’s no-answer order
rationale: Both narrate silence and no answering word because the king had ordered no answer. The particular stated reason is retained instead of an invented account of the audience’s unspoken beliefs.

relationship: The torn-garment delegation reports the envoy’s words to Hezekiah
rationale: Both name the returning officials, torn garments or tunics, and their report of Rhapsakes’s or Rapsakes’ words. Joash and Joach, and Somnas’s differing title detail, remain as supplied.

relationship: Hezekiah’s torn garments, sackcloth and Lord-house visit follow the report
rationale: Both describe Hezekiah hearing, tearing his garments, putting on sackcloth and entering or going up to the Lord’s house. Their particular mourning and movement sequence remains the narrated response to the report.

relationship: The sackcloth-clothed delegation is sent to Isaiah son of Amos
rationale: Both name Eliakim, Somnas and priestly elders sent in sackcloth to Isaiah son of Amos. The repeated delegation and recipient are explicit without an additional personal-name identification from another setting.

relationship: The distress-day message uses the woman-without-birth-strength comparison
rationale: Both messages attribute to Hezekiah a day of distress and a birth image involving insufficient strength. Kings’s children-and-birth-pains wording and Isaiah’s woman-in-labor form remain distinct rather than a rewritten identical metaphor.

relationship: The living-God reproach leads to a request to pray for those remaining
rationale: Both messages invoke what the Lord hears of the Assyrian envoy’s reproach and call for prayer or pleading for those remaining. The request is not itself turned into a narrator’s report that Isaiah had already prayed.

relationship: The royal servants arrive at Isaiah in both accounts
rationale: Both explicitly report the king’s servants coming to Isaiah after the delegation is sent. The short arrival notice is tied to the same named embassy without inventing a second journey.

relationship: The Lord’s answer says not to fear the envoys’ words
rationale: Both have Isaiah relay the Lord’s do-not-fear answer concerning the Assyrian representatives’ words. Kings’s young-servants and blasphemed wording and Isaiah’s envoys and reproached-Me wording retain their different terms.

relationship: The spirit, report, return and sword outcome are announced together
rationale: Both Lord-speeches announce a spirit placed within the king, hearing a report, returning home and a sword death in his own land. This preserves the announced sequence without importing an independent psychological or political explanation.

relationship: The envoy returns to Lomna before the Ethiopian-king report
rationale: Both place the returning envoy with the Assyrian king at Lomna and connect the scene to the Tharaka report in the following words. Kings expressly states departure from Lachish; that detail is not supplied to Isaiah’s differently divided sentence.

relationship: The Tharaka report is followed by messengers sent to Hezekiah
rationale: Both name Tharaka king of the Ethiopians in a report of hostile action and then messengers to Hezekiah. Fighting and besieging retain their supplied wording, and the report is not made a separately narrated completed battle.

relationship: The second message challenges reliance on God’s protection of Jerusalem
rationale: Both messages tell Hezekiah not to be misled by the assurance that Jerusalem will not be handed to Assyria. Kings’s lift-you-up wording remains distinct from Isaiah’s deceive-you wording, and the opposing speaker’s claim stays attributed.

relationship: The destructive history of Assyrian kings is invoked as a threat
rationale: Both speeches invoke what Assyrian kings did to lands or the earth as an argument against rescue. Their expansive territorial language remains the message’s rhetoric rather than a new independently verified catalogue of conquests.

relationship: Gozan, Charran and Raphes recur in the defeated-gods challenge
rationale: Both speeches name Gozan, Charran and Raphes while challenging whether their gods rescued them. Kings’s sons of Edem in Thaesthen and Isaiah’s country of Themad remain different final clauses without a new personal or geographical harmonization.

relationship: The where-are-the-kings challenge repeats a bounded city list
rationale: Both speeches ask where the rulers of Aimath and Arphad or Arphath and the further named places are. Seppharouain, Ana and Ava remain Kings’s forms alongside Isaiah’s Seppharim, Anag and Ougaua, without certifying each equation.

relationship: Hezekiah opens the received message before the Lord
rationale: Both narrate Hezekiah receiving the messengers’ written material and opening it before the Lord. Kings additionally mentions reading and going up to the Lord’s house; its plural letters and Isaiah’s singular document are not made identical.

relationship: Hezekiah’s prayer names the cherubim-seated Creator as God alone
rationale: Both identify the praying Hezekiah and address Israel’s God seated upon cherubim, God alone over the kingdoms and maker of heaven and earth. The distinct address titles and territorial terms are preserved rather than expanded into an additional quoted prayer.

relationship: The prayer asks divine hearing and sight of Sennacherib’s reproach
rationale: Both petitions ask the Lord to hear or look at Sennacherib’s words against the living God. Kings explicitly includes inclining the ear and opening the eyes; those words remain its own fuller prayer wording.

relationship: The prayer acknowledges the Assyrian kings’ devastation
rationale: Both prayers acknowledge that Assyrian kings truly devastated nations or the inhabited world and its country. The acknowledgement remains part of Hezekiah’s prayer, without harmonizing the different territorial scope into a new historical total.

relationship: Burned gods are contrasted with divine status as human-made wood and stone
rationale: Both prayers say the burned objects were not gods but human handiwork of wood and stone. The particular distinction answers the hostile comparison without supplying an unreported material inventory.

relationship: The rescue petition seeks worldwide knowledge that the Lord alone is God
rationale: Both prayers ask salvation from the threatening hand so the kingdoms of the earth know God’s uniqueness. Kings’s his-hand and Isaiah’s their-hand remain their actual pronominal forms.

relationship: The answer expressly names the prayer about Sennacherib as heard
rationale: Both accounts name Isaiah son of Amos and the Lord’s answer that He heard Hezekiah’s prayer about Sennacherib. Sent-to-Hezekiah and Isaiah-was-sent retain their different narrative agency wording.

relationship: Daughter Zion’s contempt and Jerusalem’s head-shaking recur
rationale: Both oracles describe virgin daughter Zion despising or sneering and daughter Jerusalem shaking her head at the addressee. Their different verbal tenses remain as supplied, without a new separately narrated action by named women.

relationship: The reproach and raised voice address Israel’s Holy One with different eye clauses
rationale: Both oracles ask whom the addressee reproached and against whom he raised his voice, naming Israel’s Holy One. Kings says he lifted his eyes on high against Him; Isaiah says he did not lift them toward Him. That polarity difference is not reconciled.

relationship: The messenger reproach is followed by a Lebanon-and-chariot boast
rationale: Both oracles quote chariot ascent, Lebanon and the cutting of cedar and cypress after reproach through messengers. Kings’s melon, farthest-part and Carmel wording remains distinct from Isaiah’s woodland-height clause without translating or replacing those terms.

relationship: Water boasts share drying language while preserving different preceding actions
rationale: Kings quotes cooling and drinking foreign waters before drying rivers of enclosure; Isaiah quotes laying a bridge and drying waters and their gatherings. The bounded water-and-drying parallel does not equate the different actions or independently identify the rivers.

relationship: Divine forming or arranging concerns the outcome of fortified places
rationale: Both oracles attribute the outcome involving fortified cities to divine forming or arranging and present bringing or showing. Kings’s exiles of fighting men and Isaiah’s desolation wording remain distinct, without rewriting either into a shared technical conquest formula.

relationship: Weakened hands and grass imagery describe the defeated inhabitants
rationale: Both oracles connect failing hands with grass imagery, including grass upon roofs. Kings’s cowering, shame and trampling clauses and Isaiah’s withering and wild-grass wording are retained as their own details.

relationship: Divine knowledge covers rest or sitting and going out and coming in
rationale: Both oracles claim knowledge of the addressee’s rest or sitting, going out and coming in. Kings additionally includes anger against Me in this unit; that clause is not inserted into Isaiah’s shorter knowledge statement.

relationship: Nose restraint and lip bridle accompany the promised reversal of the road
rationale: Both oracles connect wrath rising to God with restraint at nose and lips and turning back by the incoming road. Hooks in nostrils and muzzle in nose remain different supplied images rather than one newly certified instrument.

relationship: The three-year agricultural sign preserves different first-year provisions
rationale: Both signs describe provision in this year and the second, followed by sowing, harvest and vineyards in the third. Kings’s self-growing and sprouting food differ from Isaiah’s what-you-have-sown and what-remains wording; the shared sequence does not reconcile the crops.

relationship: The remaining Judeans are pictured with growth below and above
rationale: Both promises describe remaining people of Judah or Judea growing below and above. Kings specifies taking root downward and bearing fruit upward; Isaiah has root below and seed above, without fruit and seed being silently exchanged.

relationship: Jerusalem and Zion’s escaping remnant are attributed to the Lord’s zeal
rationale: Both promises name those remaining or escaping from Jerusalem and Mount Zion and the zeal of the Lord of hosts or Sabaoth accomplishing it. The supplied forms are preserved without counting an unreported remnant population.

relationship: The city-entry, projectile, shield and siegework prohibitions recur
rationale: Both Lord-speeches deny the Assyrian king entry, a projectile, a shield and siegework against the city. Arrow and missile, and pouring a siege ramp and surrounding with siegework, retain their different wording.

relationship: The king’s return is assigned the road by which he came
rationale: Both oracles state return by the incoming way. Kings also repeats that he shall not enter the city; that additional clause remains Kings’s own wording rather than a second sentence inserted into Isaiah.

relationship: Protection of the city is grounded in God and David His servant
rationale: Both Lord-speeches promise shielding the city for God’s own sake and David His servant’s sake. Isaiah also says to save it; the particular stated grounds are retained without supplying another dynastic pledge.

relationship: The angel strikes one hundred eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp
rationale: Both report an angel of the Lord striking one hundred eighty-five thousand in Assyria’s camp and dead bodies found upon rising early. Kings additionally says by night; no independent cause of death or further casualty arithmetic is introduced.

relationship: The Assyrian king withdraws and resides in Nineveh
rationale: Both accounts report the Assyrian king turning or returning, going away and living in Nineveh. Kings names Sennacherib in this unit; no unreported journey duration or route is added.

relationship: The temple assassination and Asordan’s succession have corresponding named notices
rationale: Both name the sons Adramelech and Sarasar striking their father during worship and his son Asordan succeeding. Neserach and Nasarach, sword and swords, and Ararat and Armenia remain the different supplied forms without an independent geographical equation.

relationship: The David-grounded city-shielding promise is repeated in the healing answer
rationale: Both Lord-speeches promise to shield the city for God’s own sake and David His servant’s sake. The later answer additionally promises fifteen years and rescue from Assyria; those healing-context clauses remain distinct from the earlier city oracle.

relationship: The Lord’s angel strikes the Assyrian camp in a second parallel account
rationale: Kings gives the angelic camp strike and its one-hundred-eighty-five-thousand figure; Chronicles reports the Lord sending an angel against warriors, rulers and commanders in that camp. Chronicles’s categories and later return are not made an independent confirmation of Kings’s exact casualty count.

relationship: Hezekiah’s deathly illness receives Isaiah’s household-order warning
rationale: Both name Hezekiah’s illness to death and Isaiah son of Amos bringing the Lord’s instruction to arrange his house because he is dying and shall not live. The shared warning is distinguished from the subsequent changed response.

relationship: Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and prays
rationale: Both narrate the same named king turning his face toward the wall and praying to the Lord. The particular posture and action are retained without adding prayer words absent from these short units.

relationship: The remembrance prayer invokes true conduct and ends in the king’s tears
rationale: Both prayers ask the Lord to remember Hezekiah’s walk in truth, his heart and his pleasing conduct, followed by his weeping. Full heart and true heart, and bitterly and greatly, remain their respective terms and his self-description remains speech.

relationship: The Lord’s renewed word comes to Isaiah after the prayer
rationale: Both report the Lord’s word coming to Isaiah before the healing answer. Kings additionally locates him in the middle courtyard; that location is not supplied to Isaiah’s shorter introduction.

relationship: The reply explicitly acknowledges Hezekiah’s prayer and tears
rationale: Both replies invoke the God of David and say the prayer was heard and tears seen. Kings also promises healing and a third-day visit to the Lord’s house; Isaiah’s fifteen years in this unit is not used to erase Kings’s different division of the answer.

relationship: Added fifteen years and rescue from Assyria accompany the city’s protection
rationale: Both replies promise fifteen added years, rescue from the Assyrian king and protection of the city. Kings additionally names God’s own sake and David’s sake here; those grounds are not inserted into Isaiah’s shorter protection clause.

relationship: The fig-cake direction is connected with recovery in both illness accounts
rationale: Kings directs a cake of figs placed on the ulcer and says he will recover; Isaiah directs crushing and applying the fig cake and promises health. The different procedural wording remains a particular narrated instruction rather than general medical advice or an independently supplied mechanism.

relationship: The Lord-house visit is connected with a sign using different grammatical forms
rationale: Kings has Hezekiah ask what sign proves healing and a third-day Lord-house visit; Isaiah has him state This is the sign that he will go up. The question-versus-statement and third-day differences are preserved instead of rewritten as the same quotation.

relationship: Same-chapter The shadow sign is read beside the narrated ten-step return
rationale: Isaiah announces a Lord-given sign in which the shadow will advance ten steps if it returns ten steps; the later notice narrates a backward ten-step return after his cry. The actual advance-and-if-return wording is retained rather than converted into an unquoted either-or choice.

relationship: Same-chapter Hezekiah’s requested backward ten steps correspond to the reported return
rationale: Hezekiah says inclining ten steps is easy and asks for ten steps backward; the next notice reports the shadow returning backward ten steps. This links the stated request and reported outcome without an astronomical calculation or a new clock mechanism.

relationship: The ten-step reversal retains distinct shadow and sun descriptions
rationale: Kings reports Isaiah crying to the Lord and the shadow returning backward ten steps on the stairway. Isaiah speaks of turning the sun back and its going up ten steps previously descended by the shadow, preserving its father’s-house clause without equating every movement statement.

relationship: The Babylonian royal message follows news of Hezekiah’s illness
rationale: Both narrate a Babylonian king sending letters after hearing Hezekiah was ill. Marodachbaladan son of Baladan with manaa and Marodach son of Laadan with envoys and gifts remain their actual forms; Isaiah also states recovery, without a new name or gift-term equation.

relationship: Hezekiah rejoices and exhibits his stores and treasury equipment
rationale: Both narrate Hezekiah rejoicing and showing silver, gold and treasury equipment, with nothing in his house withheld. Nechotha and nekhotha and the differing spice, oil and storeroom lists remain distinct, without independently translating the store names or assigning the final authority clause to Isaiah.

relationship: Isaiah asks about the visitors and Hezekiah names distant Babylon
rationale: Both report Isaiah’s questions about what the men said and where they came from, answered as a distant land, Babylon. The quoted answer identifies their stated origin without reconstructing a travel route or unreported negotiations.

relationship: The king says the visitors saw everything, including treasury contents
rationale: Both have Isaiah ask what was seen and Hezekiah answer that everything in his house and the treasury things were shown or seen. The broad answer remains his report rather than a separately audited item-by-item inventory.

relationship: Isaiah introduces the Lord’s word after the treasury examination
rationale: Both have Isaiah tell Hezekiah to hear the Lord’s word before the Babylon warning. Isaiah’s Lord Sabaoth title remains its own fuller address, while the target is the corresponding particular speech introduction.

relationship: The Babylon treasury warning preserves different concluding clauses
rationale: Both predict house possessions and accumulated ancestral goods going to Babylon. Kings concludes that no word the Lord spoke will be left over; Isaiah says nothing will be left behind. Their word-versus-goods clauses remain distinct rather than a rewritten identical prediction.

relationship: The prediction explicitly concerns descendants becoming palace eunuchs
rationale: Both predict sons or children begotten by Hezekiah being taken as eunuchs in the Babylonian king’s house. The prediction is retained without independently naming the descendants or asserting a particular later man’s identity.

relationship: Hezekiah calls the Lord’s word good and asks peace in his days
rationale: Both responses call the Lord’s spoken word good and request peace in Hezekiah’s days. Isaiah additionally names righteousness; neither response is expanded into a narrator’s judgment of the king’s hidden motives.

relationship: Hezekiah’s waterworks receive corresponding city-water notices
rationale: Kings’s closing notice names the fountain, aqueduct and bringing water into the city; Chronicles specifically describes blocking Gihon’s upper outlet and directing water toward David’s city. The bounded waterworks connection does not establish an independently surveyed engineering route.

relationship: Hezekiah’s remaining deeds are referred to written royal records
rationale: Both closing notices refer Hezekiah’s remaining deeds to written accounts; Kings cites Judah’s royal chronicles, while Chronicles names Isaiah’s prophecy and the Kings of Judah and Israel. The citations are not certified as one recovered book or claimed independently read.

relationship: Hezekiah’s burial and Manasseh’s succession close both accounts
rationale: Both narrate Hezekiah lying down with his fathers and his son Manasseh succeeding. David’s city and the ascent to the tombs of David’s sons retain their different burial descriptions, without a newly fixed tomb location.

relationship: Manasseh’s twelve-year accession and fifty-five-year reign correspond
rationale: Both give Manasseh twelve years old when he became king and fifty-five years reigning in Jerusalem. Kings additionally names his mother Opsiba; no maternal name is inserted into Chronicles’s shorter heading.

relationship: Manasseh’s evil is compared with the removed nations’ abominations
rationale: Both assess Manasseh’s evil by the abominations of nations the Lord removed or destroyed before Israel. The repeated royal judgment preserves each description without inventing an additional list of specific rites.

relationship: Rebuilt high places and heavenly-host service reverse Hezekiah’s reform
rationale: Both name rebuilding the high places Hezekiah pulled down, groves and service to heaven’s host. Kings’s altar for Baal and Ahab comparison remain distinct from Chronicles’s pillars for the Baals, without exchanging the objects or their number.

relationship: The Lord-house altar building is set beside the Jerusalem-name promise
rationale: Both juxtapose Manasseh building in the Lord’s house with the Lord’s promise to place His name in Jerusalem. Kings’s singular altar and Chronicles’s plural altars, and Chronicles’s for-ever clause, remain their actual different wording.

relationship: Heavenly-host worship structures are placed in both courts
rationale: Both locate an altar or altars for heaven’s host in the two courts of the Lord’s house. The shared object of worship and two-court setting are retained while Kings’s singular altar is not silently pluralized.

relationship: Child-fire and divinatory practices form corresponding provocation lists
rationale: Both describe passing children through fire, divinatory practices and appointed practitioners, culminating in evil provoking the Lord. Kings’s sons and particular charmer-and-knowing-ones terms remain distinct from Chronicles’s location and fuller practitioner list, without new technical glosses.

relationship: The installed image contrasts with the perpetual house-and-Jerusalem name promise
rationale: Both juxtapose Manasseh’s installed carved object with God’s word to David and Solomon about His name in the chosen house and Jerusalem for ever. Kings’s grove image and Chronicles’s carved and cast object wording remain distinct without independently deciding how many separate images each term denotes.

relationship: Remaining in the ancestral land is tied to keeping Moses’s commands
rationale: Both divine speeches promise not to shake Israel’s foot from the ancestral land in connection with doing what God commanded through Moses. Their different condition wording and commandment or law-ordinance-judgment lists remain as supplied.

relationship: Manasseh’s leading astray is assessed as exceeding the earlier nations’ evil
rationale: Both name Manasseh leading his people into evil beyond the nations the Lord removed before Israel. Kings’s did-not-listen clause and Chronicles’s explicit Judah and Jerusalem audience remain distinct rather than added to the other notice.

relationship: Same-chapter The prophet-word introduction receives its particular Manasseh judgment content
rationale: The Lord’s speech through His servants the prophets introduces the following charge against Manasseh and announced Jerusalem-Judah disasters. The actual recorded oracle is linked without assigning an unprovided name to each prophet.

relationship: Same-chapter The oracle’s worse-than-Amorite charge recalls the narrative’s worse-than-nations judgment
rationale: The oracle accuses Manasseh of evil worse than the Amorite and causing Judah to sin; the earlier narrator already says he led them beyond the nations’ evil. The particular Amorite comparison is not broadened into a claim that every named nation is identical.

relationship: The both-ears-resound judgment formula recurs for a different threatened house or people
rationale: The Jerusalem-Judah disaster announcement says both ears of its hearer will ring; the earlier word to Samuel says both ears of hearers will resound before Eli-house judgment. The shared hearing formula does not merge their different addressees or events.

relationship: The weight of Ahab’s house recalls the specific earlier dynastic judgment
rationale: The Jerusalem oracle invokes Samaria’s measure and Ahab’s house’s weight; the earlier oracle explicitly announces calamities and destruction against Ahab’s house. The connection retains the supplied measure, weight and alabaster-jar imagery without importing a different building-tool or bowl translation.

relationship: The threatened handing over and plunder is read beside Jerusalem’s later deportation
rationale: The oracle threatens the remnant with enemies and plunder; the later narrative explicitly deports Jerusalem’s rulers, fighting men and craftsmen to Babylon. The particular subsequent dispossession is compared without claiming every clause or enemy is independently exhausted by that one event.

relationship: Judah’s stated provocation since Egypt is compared with Israel’s earlier fall explanation
rationale: The Jerusalem oracle gives evil and provocation since the fathers’ exodus as grounds; the earlier Israel explanation names sin against the God who brought them from Egypt and following nations’ ordinances. Judah’s threat and Israel’s fall remain distinct settings.

relationship: The later judgment explanation explicitly recalls Manasseh’s innocent blood in Jerusalem
rationale: Kings says Manasseh filled Jerusalem with innocent blood; the later Judah explanation names Manasseh’s sins and repeats filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. The stated connection adds no victim identities or unreported casualty total.

relationship: Manasseh’s remaining deeds and sins receive differently scoped record citations
rationale: Kings cites Judah’s royal chronicles for Manasseh’s deeds and sin; Chronicles refers to accounts of his deeds, prayer, seers and pre-return sins. Those citations retain their different contents and works, without claiming the externally cited records were read.

relationship: The garden burial is followed by Amon the son’s succession
rationale: Both narrate Manasseh’s death, burial in his house’s garden and his son Amon succeeding. Kings additionally calls it Oza’s garden; that supplied name is not added to Chronicles or replaced with a different tomb description.

relationship: Amon’s twenty-two-year accession and two-year reign agree
rationale: Both give Amon twenty-two at accession and two years reigning in Jerusalem. Kings’s mother Mesollam daughter of Arous from Jeteba remains an additional clause rather than a maternal identity supplied to Chronicles.

relationship: Amon’s evil is explicitly compared with his father Manasseh
rationale: Both assess Amon as doing evil as Manasseh his father had done. Chronicles additionally specifies sacrifice and service to the father’s idols; that further detail is not inserted into Kings’s shorter assessment.

relationship: The father’s idols are served in the corresponding Amon descriptions
rationale: Kings says Amon served and bowed to the idols his father served; Chronicles says he sacrificed to and served the idols his father made. Served-versus-made and bowing-versus-sacrifice remain distinct clauses rather than identical activity lists.

relationship: Same-chapter Abandoning the Lord follows the specified service to the father’s idols
rationale: The narrator says Amon abandoned the God of his fathers and did not walk in His way after naming service and bowing to his father’s idols. The explicit opposed allegiance language interprets that particular preceding conduct without adding another unnamed cult act.

relationship: Amon’s servants attack him in his house
rationale: Both locate action by Amon’s own servants against him in his house. Kings explicitly narrates conspiracy and putting the king to death; Chronicles says they attacked and struck him. No unreported weapon or additional location is added.

relationship: The people strike the attackers and appoint Josiah the son
rationale: Both have the people of the land strike Amon’s attackers and make his son Josiah king in his place. The actual retaliating group and succeeding son remain explicit without adding a separately named regent.

relationship: Same-chapter Amon’s closing deeds citation belongs to his named earlier regnal notice
rationale: The closure cites Amon’s remaining deeds in Judah’s royal chronicles; the earlier heading names Amon, his accession age and two-year Jerusalem reign. This identifies the particular regnal subject without claiming the cited external chronicles were recovered or read.

relationship: Josiah’s succession is followed by his own Jerusalem regnal heading
rationale: The Amon burial notice again names Josiah his son succeeding; the next chapter’s heading gives Josiah’s accession age, reign and mother. Oza’s garden remains Amon’s burial location rather than a newly inferred burial for Josiah.
